summary: The toy shows an animal cell dividing by mitosis, phase by phase, in the order and with the events a biology textbook gives. The cell is a diagram: four chromosomes stand for a human cell's 46, and the parts are drawn clear and simple.

claims.claim: Prophase: the chromatin condenses into chromosomes of two sister chromatids, the nucleolus disappears and the centrosomes move toward opposite poles.
claims.how: Thin chromatin threads draw into eight solid chromatids (four chromosomes, sisters side by side); the nucleolus shrinks away; the two centrosomes travel round the nucleus to the poles.

sources.title: Biology 2e, 10.2 The Cell Cycle
sources.says: The sister chromatids begin to coil more tightly … the centrosomes begin to move to opposite poles.

claims.claim: Prometaphase: the nuclear envelope breaks into pieces and spindle microtubules reach the kinetochores.
claims.how: The envelope comes apart in twelve pieces; a fiber grows from each pole to each chromatid's kinetochore.

sources.title: Biology 2e, 10.2 The Cell Cycle
sources.says: The remnants of the nuclear envelope fragment further … Each sister chromatid develops a protein structure called a kinetochore.

claims.note: In the cell the envelope breaks into many small vesicles; the toy shows twelve large pieces so they read as pieces.

claims.claim: Metaphase: the chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate midway between the poles.
claims.how: The chromosomes move to the plane between the poles, each sister attached to its own pole.

sources.title: Biology 2e, 10.2 The Cell Cycle
sources.says: All the chromosomes are aligned in a plane called the metaphase plate, or the equatorial plane, roughly midway between the two poles.

claims.claim: Anaphase: the sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles, and the cell elongates.
claims.how: Each pair of sisters parts; each moves as a solid piece toward its pole as its fiber shortens; the poles move apart and the cell stretches.

sources.title: Biology 2e, 10.2 The Cell Cycle
sources.says: The cohesin proteins degrade, and the sister chromatids separate at the centromere … The cell becomes visibly elongated (oval shaped) as the polar microtubules slide.

claims.claim: Telophase and cytokinesis: new nuclear envelopes form round each set of chromosomes, which decondense, and a contractile ring of actin pinches the cell in two at the cleavage furrow.
claims.how: New nuclei fade in round the chromosomes at each pole; a red ring at the equator closes as the membrane pinches into two cells.

sources.title: Biology 2e, 10.2 The Cell Cycle
sources.says: the chromosomes reach the opposite poles and begin to decondense … Nuclear envelopes form around the chromosomes … A contractile ring composed of actin filaments forms just inside the plasma membrane … This fissure is called the cleavage furrow.

claims.note: The chromatids switch to the new nuclei's chromatin as the envelopes form, rather than unwinding visibly.

claims.claim: A human cell has 46 chromosomes; the toy shows four, two pairs of homologs (each a slightly different shade).
claims.how: Four chromosomes, two long and two short, in two shades of pink and two of blue.

sources.title: How many chromosomes do people have?
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus Genetics (U.S. National Library of Medicine)
sources.says: In humans, each cell normally contains 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46.

simplified: Four chromosomes stand for 46; their banding is decorative, not a real karyotype.
Each daughter gets one centrosome; the copy that appears beside it at the end stands for the duplication in the next S phase.
Spindle fibers are drawn as a few lines (a real spindle has thousands of microtubules) and astral microtubules are left out.
Only one daughter is followed: it grows back into the starting cell (G1), so the toy can play again; the other drifts away.
The whole division takes about 18 seconds; in a human cell mitosis takes about an hour.
